Reliability is a budget conversation — not an uptime aspiration
blocks.sub: Signed SLOs, budget-gated releases and incident craft that closes its actions

blocks.x: SRE & Reliability Engineering is delivered by an Achala practice team that stays through industrialization. Achala stages every migration with reconciliation gates: the old system and the new one run side by side until the numbers match. Rollback plans are written before cutover, not after incidents. Who this is for: CTOs and infrastructure leads carrying estate cost, and program boards that cannot afford a failed migration.
The practice covers SLO design, alert quality (precision matters more than volume), toil elimination, and the incident-review loop that converts every failure into either a guardrail or a test.
Below: the failure modes that make SRE programs decorative, the reference architecture of budget-gated delivery, and the console that keeps the honest numbers.

widgets.title: Incident lifecycle — click stages for the rehearsal contract

stages.name: Detect
stages.detail: Detection is a burn-rate breach on a journey SLO — pages carry the journey, the burn multiple and the dashboard link; symptom-only alerts were deleted with a ledger entry.

stages.name: Respond
stages.detail: Incident commander, ops lead, comms lead — roles rehearsed in game days; the on-call acts from the runbook, not from memory.

stages.name: Mitigate
stages.detail: Mitigation prefers reversible actions (rollback, feature flag, shed) over heroic fixes; the timeline logs every action with its evidence.

stages.name: Communicate
stages.detail: Customer-impact statements use the same arithmetic as the SLO (affected journeys × duration × volume) — no adjectives without numbers.

stages.name: Learn
stages.detail: Blameless review within a week; remediation items with owners and deadlines verified by drill; repeat classes escalate to the governance backlog.

widgets.note: The lifecycle is rehearsed quarterly in game days — the incident that surprises nobody is the one that costs least.

blocks.sub: SLOs, budget-gated releases and incident craft, the system that makes reliability tradable

blocks.x: Reliability programs become decorative when SLOs are aspirations: published, admired and gating nothing. The working system treats the error budget as currency, every service carries a signed SLO document (what is measured, by whom, at what threshold), the calculator tracks burn live, and budget exhaustion freezes releases automatically in CI, converting the reliability-versus-velocity argument from a meeting into a number. The freeze is the discipline: teams may buy budget back with reliability work, and the trade is visible to everyone.

Incident craft is the second half: incident command with named roles trained before the page, chaos drills monthly and scoped (a drill that takes the estate down teaches nothing but fear), and blameless reviews whose actions carry owners and dates, reviewed in the same meeting as the budget, because actions that never close are how programs become decorative. The console reads SLO adherence, budget burn and drill results; the review reads trends, not anecdotes.

items: Every service: what, who, threshold, signed by the business owner.
Exhaustion freezes deploys in CI; the trade is a number, not a meeting.
Drills sized to teach, rehearsed against production shapes.
Every review action carries a name and a date, reviewed to closure.

SLOs nobody gates on, error budgets nobody spends, reviews that read averages. We make the budget a currency: releases freeze on burn, gates read adherence, and the console shows the numbers the review actually argues with.
How do error budgets change release behavior?

A burn above policy freezes feature releases until the budget recovers, the freeze is automatic and dated, so the trade-off between velocity and reliability is priced in real time, not argued after the incident.
How do you pick SLOs that teams actually respect?
SLOs are set at the user journey, not the server: adherence targets signed with product owners, measured in the console and revised quarterly. A target nobody argues with is a target nobody reads.
What does MTTR improvement actually come from?

Incident craft: paging that reaches the right human, runbooks rehearsed as drills, and postmortems whose actions are gated to closure. The 58→31 minute drop comes from the drill calendar, not from hope.
Can this overlay our existing on-call and CI?

Yes, the integration surface is observability, CI and paging: budgets read from your monitors, gates sit in your pipeline, and paging carries the budget context so the responder knows what is at stake.
